# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# Critical Reading: Two-Year Follow-up of the Varden Trial and Halden Subset

**Bottom line:** This is the most informative paper in the series. It answers the durability question with the right kind of data, it corrects the meta-analysis using that review's own supplementary table, and it is candid about its limits. Its weak points are the mediation analysis and the evidence for decay. The mediation analysis is presented more confidently than its design allows, and part of the meetings "effect" may be an accounting identity rather than better work. The measured decline in the gain may be partly caused by control offices improving rather than treated offices fading.

## 1. Arithmetic

**Checks that hold:**
- Per hour on timesheets: 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098, so +9.8%. Correct.
- Per hour on system logs: 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085, so +8.5%. Correct.
- Halden continuers: 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866 (−13.4%), and 96.8 / 86.6 = 1.118 (+11.8%). Correct.
- Mediation shares: 47 + 18 + 35 = 100. Correct.
- "Declined by about a quarter": 12.5 → 9.8 on timesheets is −22%. Fair.

**Two figures that need explanation:**
- **Cost per contact.** Adding 12% more staff at unchanged pay to handle the same demand raises *labour* cost per contact by about 12%. The stated 9% only works if labour is about three-quarters of total cost per contact. That is plausible but unstated.
- **Control-office meeting time.** It averaged 7.2 → 7.0 hours. Yet two of the seven control offices cut theirs from 7.1 to 5.0 after their meeting audit. If all offices are weighted equally, those two alone would pull the average down by about 0.6 hours. The other five offices must therefore have *increased* meetings by roughly half an hour each, or the averages are weighted differently, or the month-24 figure was taken before the audit offices were fully counted. This should be clarified.

## 2. What it does well

- **The right design for durability.** It uses record-based output, actual hours, a randomised comparison and two years of follow-up. These are exactly the standards Varga and Holm demanded.
- **A stricter hours measure.** The system logs add a second hours measure to address unrecorded work, and the conclusion holds on the stricter measure.
- **A prespecified mediation analysis.** It was registered at month 11, before the 24-month outcomes were available.
- **Baseline meeting times.** Treated offices started at 7.4 hours and controls at 7.2. This resolves my earlier concern that the month-six gap might have existed before the trial.
- **The meta-analysis's long studies.** It shows that all four studies with long follow-up were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. That confirms the suspicion I raised about the review's duration claim, and it removes the basis for "novelty can be set aside."
- **Candour about counter offices.** The counter arm was stopped because service got worse, and the paper reports that plainly as a result.
- **Honest framing of the Halden subset.** It calls the continuing Halden organisations "survivors twice over" and treats their figures as an upper bound.
- **The control-office observation.** It reports the meeting audit even though it complicates the authors' own story, and it states clearly what the trial cannot answer.

## 3. Problems

**The mediation result is stated too strongly.**
- The summary says the test "confirms" meetings as a mechanism. The paper's own limitations section concedes that mediators were not randomised and that confounding between mediators and outcome cannot be ruled out. "Supports" would be accurate; "confirms" is not.
- **Not an independent replication.** The hypothesis came from these same seven offices. Registering the test before the outcomes were known removes freedom in how the analysis is run. It does not give an independent replication, which was the point of Varga and Holm's objection.
- **Too few clusters.** "A larger sample of office-months" overstates the information available. Office-months within an office are correlated, so there are still effectively 7 versus 7 clusters. The confidence intervals, such as 28–66%, may be too narrow unless a small-cluster correction was used.
- **Possible accounting identity.** If meeting time counts in the hours denominator, cutting meetings while keeping case work steady raises output per hour *by definition*. "Meetings explain 47%" would then largely mean "meetings were hours that produced no cases closed." That is a useful finding, but it is not evidence that staff worked faster or better. It also assumes meetings had no value that the output measure misses, such as coordination, training or quality. The appeal overturn rate edged from 3.1% to 3.2% against 3.0% in controls. That is a small change, but it is the only quality signal available.
- **What do the logs measure?** The paper says log-in time "records time staff are working on cases." If meetings are not in log time, the meetings pathway cannot work mechanically on that denominator. Yet log hours fell 11%, almost as much as timesheet hours. That is hard to reconcile with meetings accounting for about 3.5 of the roughly 4.5 hours cut, unless staff stay logged in during meetings. The paper needs to say exactly what log time includes.

**The evidence of decay is weaker, and possibly contaminated.**
- **Overlapping intervals.** The 9-month interval (6.9 to 18.4) and the 24-month interval (4.6 to 15.2) overlap heavily. The decline is a point-estimate pattern, not a statistically established change. "Consistent with some fading" is fair; "declined by about a quarter" is stated too firmly.
- **Contaminated controls.** The meeting audit in two control offices from month 15 is contamination. If their output per hour rose about 4%, the control average rose too, and the difference-in-differences gain shrank *without the treated offices changing*. Part of the apparent decay may be control offices catching up. Treated offices' own trend in output per hour, or an estimate excluding the two audit offices, would separate the two explanations.
- **A positive implication.** If contamination is the cause, the true effect of the reduced schedule against an untouched control is somewhat larger than 8.5%. Meanwhile the audit offices hint that part of the gain is available without cutting hours, as the authors note.

**The audit observation itself is weak.**
- It covers two self-selected offices and compares them with their own previous six months.
- Seasonality and regression to the mean (offices may audit when they feel unusually inefficient) are not addressed. The authors' hedging is appropriate.

**The Halden subset is filtered again.**
- Only 14 of the 23 organisations with records responded, and non-responders may include more that reverted or struggled.
- It is not stated whether all 11 continuing organisations have time tracking. Earlier, only 17 of the 23 had both records and time tracking.
- **A wrinkle in the work-type binary.** The marketing agency, a discretionary setting, reverted over client deadlines. Client responsiveness is a form of coverage obligation that can exist in "discretionary" sectors. This reinforces the point that the classification applies to roles, not sectors.

**Possible conflict of interest.** Okafor, an author of the original Halden paper, co-authors the Halden section. The section is candid ("survivors twice over," upper bound), so this is a note rather than a criticism.

## 4. Where the evidence now stands

| Question | Current best answer | Change from before |
|---|---|---|
| Output per actual hour, discretionary work | About +8.5–10% at 24 months (randomised, log-measured) | Narrowed; now has long-run controlled support |
| Output per worker, discretionary work | About −3% (CI −8.0 to +1.2) | Slightly worse over time; cost per case is somewhat higher |
| Durability | Gain persists to 24 months. Some decline, possibly partly from control contamination | Novelty-only explanation now unlikely; "no decay" also unsupported |
| Coverage-bound work | Stopped by the employer; restoring service needs about 12% more staff | Now settled for this setting |
| Mechanism | Meetings plausibly the largest single pathway, partly by accounting. Fatigue smaller. About a third unexplained | Upgraded from exploratory to supported, not confirmed |
| Reorganisation without cutting hours | Open. Hinted at by two offices; untested | New question |
| Wellbeing and retention | Sick days −27%, resignations roughly halved, sustained | Durable |

The extreme positions in the series have both been refuted: Halden's sector-general 23% at one end, and Varga and Holm's "entirely an artifact" at the other. What remains is a moderate, durable gain of about 9% per hour in discretionary work. Output per worker falls slightly, retention and sickness improve substantially, and coverage-bound work cannot absorb the cut without extra staff. The most useful next study would be the one this trial couldn't run: an arm that reorganises meetings and workflow *without* cutting hours. That would show whether the gain comes from fewer hours or from the reorganisation that cutting hours forces.
